titre: The Benin Bronzes: One Museum That Gives Back, One That Cannot
accroche: In 1897, the British army loots the Benin Bronzes. In 2022, the Smithsonian cedes twenty-nine to Nigeria; the British Museum cannot.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1897, a British military expedition led by Admiral Harry Rawson sacks and destroys Benin City, capital of the Kingdom of Benin, in present-day Nigeria. It is launched in reprisal for the ambush in January 1897 of a British mission, from which only two Europeans emerge alive. The victors carry off the works that adorned the royal palace and the residences of the nobility, accumulated over centuries: bronze and ivory sculptures, between 3,000 and 5,000 pieces according to Nevadomsky's estimate. Some end up in the private collections of British officials; the Foreign Office sells a large number, which land in European and American museums, and gives the British Museum a large quantity of bronze plaques.

## Two Museums, Two Regimes

More than a century later, these objects are scattered across dozens of Western museums. The British Museum holds about nine hundred of them, one of the two largest groups along with Berlin's, but its administrators, the Trustees, cannot give them back at will. The British Museum Act of 1963, a British statute, provides in section 3(4) that objects in the collections may be disposed of only in the cases the Act allows. Section 5 lists a few: duplicates, certain printed items of which a photographic copy is kept, objects judged unfit to remain in the collections, or made useless by damage.

In 2005, the High Court in London applies this text in another case. The heirs of Dr. Feldmann, whose four drawings had been stolen by the Gestapo in Brno on March 15, 1939, were asking for their return. As early as 2002, the Trustees had decided that the claim should be granted if the law allowed. The judge concludes that no moral obligation can justify a disposal contrary to section 3(4): it would take legislation, or a bona fide compromise over ownership of the drawings.

The Smithsonian took another route. On October 11, 2022, the National Museum of African Art, one of its museums, signs over ownership of twenty-nine Benin bronzes to Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments, the NCMM. Wikipedia notes for its part that the British Museum's collection of about nine hundred objects remains protected today by an act of Parliament, and that negotiations with the museum continue.

## A Question Hiding Another

The difference between the two museums is therefore not first a difference of will. The British Museum's Trustees had decided in 2002 to return the Feldmann drawings if the law allowed, and the High Court ruled that it did not. The question "should this museum return the object it holds?" often assumes, without saying so, a narrower and less visible one: does it have the power to, in the strict sense of the law that governs it? Two museums can answer the first question differently without ever having disagreed on the substance. For the Feldmann drawings, the 2005 judge says it plainly: only legislation could change the answer.

repere.texte: Section 3(4) of the British Museum Act of 1963 forbids the Trustees to dispose of an object in the collections other than under sections 5 or 9 of the Act.

carte.punch: In 1897, the British army loots the Benin Bronzes. One museum can give them back, the other cannot.
carte.idee: Looted by British troops in 1897, the Benin Bronzes are scattered across Western museums. In 2022, the Smithsonian signs over twenty-nine bronzes to Nigeria; the British Museum is bound by a 1963 law that the High Court found admitted no moral exception in 2005.

quiz.question: Why can't the British Museum return its Benin Bronzes the way the Smithsonian did in 2022?
choix: Because Nigeria gave up in 2022 on claiming the objects held in London
Because the 2005 judgment ordered the British Museum to keep all Benin objects
Because a 1963 law limits the cases in which its Trustees may dispose of an object in the collections
Because the British Museum's bronzes were not taken from Benin City in 1897
quiz.explication: The British Museum Act of 1963 leaves the Trustees only a few cases of disposal, and the High Court ruled in 2005 that no moral obligation allowed an exception, even for drawings stolen by the Gestapo. The judgment concerned those drawings, not Benin; the British Museum's Benin plaques do come from the 1897 expedition, and discussions with Nigeria continue.
